analysis.one_liner: Blocks airlines in bankruptcy from cutting union wages and working conditions outside normal bargaining rules.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Judiciary Committee: it was introduced in March 1989, got one hearing, and died without ever coming to a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the bankruptcy code, a company filing for reorganization can ask a judge to throw out its union contracts to cut costs. This bill would have put airlines in the same category as railroads: they could not change employee wages or working conditions in bankruptcy except through the bargaining process of the Railway Labor Act. It also would have forced a bankrupt airline's parent companies and affiliates into bankruptcy together, so creditors could reach assets the carrier's corporate group held elsewhere.
analysis.who_benefits: Unionized airline employees, whose wages and working conditions could no longer be rewritten by a bankruptcy judge when their airline files for Chapter 11. Railroads already have this protection; the bill would extend the same rule to airlines. It also benefits creditors, who could collect from the whole corporate family of a failed airline rather than just the bankrupt shell.

how_it_helps.text: Extends to airlines the rule that already applies to railroads: a bankruptcy trustee cannot alter employee wages or working conditions except in accordance with the Railway Labor Act, the collective bargaining law covering airlines and railroads.

Amends the bankruptcy code so the prohibition covers a debtor in possession as well as a trustee, closing the route by which an airline could shed its union contract while running the company itself in Chapter 11.

Requires that a bankrupt air carrier and every member of its controlled group of corporations file for bankruptcy together and be treated as consolidated, letting creditors reach assets held elsewhere in the corporate family.

analysis.who_pays: Airlines in financial distress, which would lose the ability to cut labor costs quickly through bankruptcy reorganization, and their corporate parents and affiliates, which could be pulled into bankruptcy and their assets opened to creditors. Cost savings from contract rejection would instead have to come through bargaining with unions.
analysis.who_pays_short: Distressed airlines and their parent companies

drawbacks.text: The bill removes a tool distressed airlines use to survive: rejecting costly labor contracts in bankruptcy can keep a carrier flying and preserve some jobs where otherwise the whole company might shut down. Creditors and other parties would also recover less if labor costs stay high during a reorganization.

Forcing every affiliate of an airline into bankruptcy together, and treating them as one company, could drag solvent subsidiaries into court and complicate reorganizations, raising the cost of credit for airline groups.
The change would apply immediately to any case filed on or after the bill's introduction date, with no transition for restructurings already in motion.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For unionized airline workers, the bill offered real protection: their contracts would survive bankruptcy unless renegotiated through normal bargaining, as railroad contracts already do. The cost falls on distressed carriers and creditors, who lose a cheaper path through Chapter 11, and some savings achieved by rejecting contracts may have kept marginal airlines alive. The design — retroactive to the date of introduction and aimed at whole corporate groups — is aggressive, and an honest supporter would concede it raises the price and risk of airline bankruptcy filings.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which held a single hearing in March 1989 and never voted to send it to the floor; it died when the Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Sen. Howard Metzenbaum introduced the bill on March 8, 1989; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the same day.
The Judiciary Committee held hearings on the bill on March 17, 1989 (printed as S.Hrg. 101-548), the only committee action it ever received.
The bill had only one cosponsor in the Senate and no further action was taken before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991, so it never came to a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Airlines and their corporate parents are better off, since they kept the ability to shed union labor costs in bankruptcy; the unionized airline workers the bill aimed to protect got nothing.

for.name: Sen. Howard M. Metzenbaum
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and secured a Judiciary Committee hearing on it.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Held one hearing on March 17, 1989 and never voted to report the bill to the Senate floor.

against.name: Airlines facing bankruptcy reorganizations
against.role: Air carriers and their corporate groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed legislation that would have kept union contracts enforceable and limited their ability to cut labor costs in Chapter 11.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Democratic sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor, and it never reached a vote, so no roll call exists to show how support or opposition split by party.

industries.note: The bill would have barred airlines in Chapter 11 from cutting union wages and working conditions outside Railway Labor Act bargaining. The savings they currently can obtain by rejecting contracts would come out of workers' pay, so their interest in keeping the tool runs against airline employees.

Bankrupt carriers would have to bring their whole controlled group into bankruptcy together, treated as one company, exposing assets held outside the carrier to creditors. This targets corporate structures that separate a money-losing airline from the rest of its family.

Creditors could reach the assets of a bankrupt air carrier's controlled group and recover more of what they are owed, a change that runs alongside creditors' and workers' shared interest in limiting asset-stripping around a failing carrier.
